meaning: A cluster of SageMaker-managed instances that stays up between jobs, is health-checked and repaired by AWS, and is scheduled by Slurm or by Amazon EKS.
A pretrained network that takes camera images and an instruction and outputs robot actions.
Fine-tuning a pretrained VLA on demonstrations from your own robot.
The batch scheduler of classic supercomputing: users submit shell scripts and it runs them on the nodes of a queue.
The Slurm command that submits a job script to a queue.
The Slurm command that launches one step of a job on the allocated nodes; HyperPod adds the --auto-resume=1 flag to it.
Slurm's name for a queue and the set of nodes that serve it.
The managed Kubernetes control plane; a HyperPod cluster supplies its worker nodes, mapped 1-to-1.
HyperPod's unit of capacity: a named set of instances of one type (or a flexible list of types) with a count and one capacity market.
An instance group that lists up to 20 instance types in priority order and falls back down the list when capacity is missing.
A prepaid SageMaker GPU reservation with a start and an end, attached to one instance group.
HyperPod's default way of filling groups: it records a target count, retries failed launches in the background and lets jobs start on the capacity that has arrived.
A set-up script HyperPod runs once on each new node.
A Kubernetes package; HyperPod's chart installs its health agent, device plug-ins and training operators on the EKS cluster.
The Kubernetes controller that turns a training job description such as a PyTorchJob into pods.
The Kubeflow Training Operator's object that describes one PyTorch training run.
The HyperPod training operator's job object, whose runPolicy carries retry counts and rules that detect a hung job.
The EC2 network device the nodes of one multi-node training job talk through.
NVIDIA's GPU diagnostic tool; its most thorough level is the longest part of a deep health check.
An optional stress test HyperPod runs on a new or replaced instance before work lands on it.
The HyperPod process on each node that watches for hardware faults and labels the node's health.
The cluster setting that lets HyperPod reboot or replace a faulty node without being asked.
The mechanism that restarts a job after its node was replaced: annotations on a Kubernetes job, or a flag on a Slurm step.
An open-source Kubernetes node autoscaler that launches nodes for pods that cannot be scheduled and removes empty ones; HyperPod runs it for you.
The object that lists which instance groups Karpenter may raise.
Karpenter's object that points at a node class and holds the rules for removing nodes.
The NodePool setting for how long Karpenter waits before removing a node it no longer needs.
HyperPod's multi-team layer on EKS: an add-on that installs Kueue and adds a cluster policy and per-team compute allocations.
A Kubernetes controller that holds a job until quota is free and then admits it.
Kueue's per-namespace queue, the one a team's jobs name in their label.
The one task governance object per cluster that holds priority classes and how idle compute is shared.
A team's quota: resources, a sharing strategy, a borrow limit and a preemption rule.
How much idle quota beyond its own allocation a team may use, in percent of that allocation.
Stopping a running task so that a higher-priority task, or the team that lent the quota, can use the compute.
A Kubernetes mark on a node that stops new pods being scheduled there.
The time Kubernetes gives a pod to stop after it is told to; the window in which a training script can write a last checkpoint.
A managed parallel file system every node mounts, used here for datasets and checkpoints.
A HyperPod feature that recovers a failed node's training state from healthy peers.
A HyperPod feature that writes checkpoints to node memory, copies them to adjacent nodes and persists them periodically to storage.
A HyperPod feature that grows and shrinks a training job by checkpointing and resuming with a different number of workers.
